awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  Rapid Lift-Based Peel Separation Masked Inverted Stereolithography 3D Printing for Urgent Procedural Planning
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader/commercial impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will be a major contribution to both the scientific understanding and the technological advance of desktop inverted vat photopolymerization 3D printing. First, the theoretical analysis of the peel process will enhance scientific understanding. Second, the experimental validation will demonstrate industry readiness of the technology. These advances will inspire other innovations in healthcare and 3D printing. High throughput 3D printing will enable trauma surgeons to benefit from 3D printed anatomic models in their planning whereas current technologies are unable to address urgent surgeries due to slow throughput. The project aims to improve the surgical outcomes of 2.5 million patients who undergo urgent procedures in the US every year. The proposed lift-based peel separation technology will provide 6X the throughput of commercial 3D printing and provide a durable competitive advantage. The business model includes the sale of the 3D printer, consumables, spare parts, and service contracts to hospitals, medical device companies, and industry. The patent-pending lift-based peel separation innovation will be at the core of commercial success. The first target customers are trauma and urgent care hospitals across the US. 

Current desktop inverted vat photopolymerization 3D printing suffers low throughput, which prevents its adoption in planning urgent surgeries. The four project objectives are centered around the development of the core technology, the Lift-Based Peel Separation system, which aims to print 6X faster than the standard. First, application of fracture mechanics and control theory to a theoretical analysis of the peel process will provide foundational understanding. Second, incorporation of force feedback and peel detection into the peel control model, together with a firmware implementation, will bring the theoretical understanding into the real world. Third, experimentation will fine-tune and validate compatibility with medical-grade resin and membrane materials. Lastly, assessment of print quality via 3D surface scanning, caliper measurements, and optical microscopy will ensure dimensional accuracy within 1 mm and satisfactory surface quality for clinical application. It is anticipated that 6X throughput will be achieved as evidenced by print times for 10 anatomic models printed using the proposed technology. Further, it is anticipated that model accuracy will be within 0.5 mm for successful application to diagnostic use. Ultimately, it is expected that the technology will be versatile as demonstrated by its compatibility with many membrane and resin materials.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF SBIR Phase I project achieved all objectives. It completed with the successful derivation and firmware implementation of the Lift-Based Peel Separation (LBPSTM) innovation, a novel way to improve the peel process in resin 3D printing. Verification proved that LBPSTM is compatible with a wide range of resin materials, but only one durable vat membrane material. Validation involved 172 printed models with a success rate of 70% at the start. The success rate rose to 95% at the end as learnings were incorporated. The 6X speed goal was achieved, but with some degradation in quality and reliability. At 3X speed, quality and reliability matched the industry standard except when related to shortcomings that were discovered in the current 3D printer design. The shortcomings laid the foundation for the proposed Phase II effort.

Meteora3D’s Phase I R&D goal was to understand, develop, verify, and validate the Lift-Based Peel System (LBPSTM) innovation, a novel way of improving the peel process in resin 3D printing. The following objectives were successfully and fully met.

  1. A simplified peel formulation was analytically derived and implemented as a simulation code. Time-integration and control theory were incorporated to derive LBPSTM motion strategies. The work revealed two distinct vat motion strategies, each having advantages and disadvantages. 

  2. A Real-Time Force-Based Optimal Motion Control (RTFBOMCTM) scheme was derived and implemented in the 3D printer firmware to command continuous-time LBPSTM motions for active control of peel and descent movements during 3D printing.

  3. LBPSTM and RTFBOMCTM were verified to be compatible with a wide range of resins, including biocompatible, transparent, opaque, rigid, and flexible resins that are used in fabricating anatomical models, medical devices, and dental models. LBPSTM was found to be compatible with only one very durable separation membrane material that can withstand repeated vat tensioning cycles.

  4. LBPSTM and RTFBOMCTM were validated by printing 172 medical and dental models. The success rate was 70% at the start and rose to 95% at the end as learnings were incorporated. The goal of printing anatomical models at 6X speed relative to the industry standard was achieved but with some degradation in quality and reliability. At 3X speed, XY dimensional accuracy, surface quality, and print reliability matched the industry standard except when related to shortcomings that were discovered in the current 3D printer design.

Meteora3D’s innovative LBPSTM and RTFBOMCTM technologies can transform the planning of 5.8 million trauma and emergency surgeries per year, advancing the health and welfare of Americans. The team’s cutting-edge approach adds a unique perspective to the scientific and technological landscape. It will serve as a foundation and inspiration for future innovation in the 3D printing field, surgical preparation field, and allied fields. Even though the US offers some of the most advanced treatment options, it has the world’s most expensive healthcare system. Meteora3D’s technology will reduce healthcare expenses by reducing operative time, blood loss, fluoroscopic use, and by contributing to superior clinical outcomes for patients, which reduces future healthcare spending. This will increase the economic competitiveness of US medical devices in the world market and improve the efficiency of the US healthcare system domestically. The timely 3D printed anatomic models enabled by Meteora3D’s cutting-edge technology are expected to reduce operating room time by 30-60 minutes or higher per case. This represents a potential operating room cost savings of over $17 billion for the 5.8 million patients based on the $3,000 saved on average per case when a 3D printed model is used. In addition, the automation features in Meteora3D’s product will reduce labor costs by up to $44,000/year. Labor costs are the biggest hurdle to widespread adoption of 3D printing at the point-of-care. Meteora3D’s innovative technology will drive increased adoption of 3D printing across US healthcare.

The Phase I R&D achieved all objectives and successfully de-risked Meteora3D’s core technology stack including the LBPSTM and RTFBOMCTM innovations. Feasibility was established, and the team demonstrated the ability to conduct high-quality, deeply technical R&D. Experimentation revealed substantial speed advantages over competition, which was the initial focus. It also revealed shortcomings that must be addressed. For helping us to achieve this major milestone, the Meteora3D team is very grateful to NSF and the SBIR program. We continue to have our sights set on one-hour surgical 3D printing including post-processing. In addition, we have recently turned our sights toward dental 3D printing, which desires speed & automation together with accuracy, and has a larger venture scale market. In the next phase, with NSF Phase II R&D support, the identified shortcomings will be addressed.
